interactions.label: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between primary and seconda

params.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between primary and secondary injury in trauma?

answers.text: Both primary and secondary injuries occur simultaneously at the moment of the traumatic event.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Secondary injury develops in the minutes to days after impact, driven by hypoxia, hypotension, and raised intracranial pressure — it does not occur at the moment of trauma.

answers.text: Secondary injury refers to damage caused by a second traumatic event, such as a subsequent fall.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Secondary injury is not a new trauma. It refers to physiological damage — such as ischaemia from hypotension — that develops after the initial impact and can be prevented by medical intervention.

answers.text: Primary injury occurs at the moment of impact and is irreversible; secondary injury develops afterwards and is preventable through timely medical care.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Primary injury (contusions, lacerations, axonal shearing) is set at impact and cannot be reversed. Secondary injury (hypoxia, hypotension, raised ICP) develops later and is the target of all trauma management.

answers.text: Primary injury is always minor; secondary injury is always more severe and occurs regardless of treatment.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Primary injury can be devastating (e.g., diffuse axonal injury). Secondary injury is important precisely because it is preventable — good clinical management stops it from developing.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review this distinction — it is the most important concept in trauma. Primary injury is irreversible; secondary injury (hypoxia, hypotension, raised ICP) is what your management prevents.
Well done. Recognising that secondary injury is preventable is the principle that drives every decision in trauma management.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic ac

params.question: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. His GCS is E1 V2 M4 (total 7). What is the most important first step in management?

answers.text: Perform an urgent CT scan to identify the intracranial lesion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CT is essential but comes after airway management. A GCS of 7 means the patient cannot protect the airway, and even brief hypoxia significantly worsens secondary brain injury.

answers.text: Secure the airway by endotracheal intubation with cervical spine control

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A GCS of 8 or below means the patient cannot protect the airway. Intubation with cervical spine control is the immediate priority — hypoxia and hypotension must be corrected before imaging.

answers.text: Administer intravenous mannitol to reduce intracranial pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Mannitol may help with raised intracranial pressure later, but airway protection comes first. Without adequate oxygenation, osmotherapy cannot prevent secondary brain injury.
Incorrect. Craniotomy may ultimately be required, but only after the airway is secure, hypoxia and hypotension are corrected, and a CT scan has confirmed the lesion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the threshold: GCS ≤ 8 means the patient cannot protect the airway. Intubation with cervical spine control comes before imaging, mannitol, or surgery.
Excellent. GCS ≤ 8 means an unprotected airway — intubate first. Correcting hypoxia and hypotension before imaging prevents secondary brain injury.

params.question: The presence of tissue bridges crossing a wound indicates that it was caused by a sharp cutting instrument.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. Tissue bridges indicate a laceration caused by blunt force, not a sharp instrument. A sharp cutting instrument produces an incised wound with clean edges and no tissue bridges — a distinction important in both clinical and medicolegal contexts.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Tissue bridges are the hallmark of a laceration caused by blunt force tearing the tissue. An incised wound from a sharp instrument has clean, smooth edges with no tissue bridges. This is a key medicolegal distinction.

interactions.label: Why does tension pneumothorax cause cardiovascular collapse in addition to respi

params.question: Why does tension pneumothorax cause cardiovascular collapse in addition to respiratory failure?

answers.text: Blood loss into the pleural space leads to hypovolaemic shock

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This describes massive haemothorax, not tension pneumothorax. In tension pneumothorax, trapped air — not blood — raises intrapleural pressure and shifts the mediastinum.

answers.text: The collapsed lung releases inflammatory mediators that cause systemic vasodilation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The cardiovascular collapse is mechanical — mediastinal shift compresses the great veins, directly reducing venous return — not an inflammatory process.

answers.text: Rib fractures associated with pneumothorax directly injure the myocardium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Tension pneumothorax does not require rib fractures. Its cardiovascular effects result from mediastinal shift compressing the great veins, not from direct cardiac injury.

answers.text: Air trapped under rising pressure shifts the mediastinum, compressing the great veins and reducing venous return

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A one-way valve traps air in the pleural space with each breath. Rising pressure collapses the lung (causing hypoxia) and shifts the mediastinum, compressing the great veins and dropping cardiac output.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: tension pneumothorax acts as a one-way valve. Trapped air raises pleural pressure, shifts the mediastinum, and compresses the great veins — that mechanical compression of venous return causes cardiovascular collapse.

Well done. Tension pneumothorax is uniquely dangerous because it triggers all three killing mechanisms of chest trauma — hypoxia, impaired ventilation, and impaired venous return from mediastinal shift.

interactions.label: A head-injured patient with a GCS of 10 is being monitored in the emergency depa

params.question: A head-injured patient with a GCS of 10 is being monitored in the emergency department. Which of the following complications, if it develops, represents a secondary brain injury that the team can still prevent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hypotension reduces cerebral perfusion and causes ischaemia — this is secondary brain injury. It develops after the initial trauma and is precisely what ongoing monitoring and resuscitation aim to prevent.
Incorrect. Diffuse axonal injury occurs at the moment of impact from rotational forces shearing nerve fibres. It is a primary injury and cannot be prevented once it has occurred.

answers.text: Cortical contusion at the site of impact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Cortical contusions are primary injuries caused by direct impact to the brain. They are set at the moment of injury and cannot be reversed.
Incorrect. A skull fracture is a primary injury from the initial impact force. It is irreversible once it has occurred.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: primary injuries (contusions, fractures, axonal injury) happen at impact and cannot be undone. Secondary injuries like hypotension-induced ischaemia develop afterwards — these are what your vigilant monitoring prevents.
Excellent. The primary injury is done. Recognising that secondary brain injury — hypoxia, hypotension, raised ICP — is preventable is the basis of all post-injury monitoring and management.
